c.tagline: Amazon gateway of the Ver-o-Peso market, mango-lined streets, and açaí.

taxi.fareNote: City taxis are metered; ride-hailing apps (Uber, 99) are widely used and usually cheaper than street taxis.

emergency.note: 193 reaches the fire brigade; 190 is the military police; 192 summons SAMU ambulances.

avoid.reason: Caution around Ver-o-Peso market and the centre after dark

hood_desc: The historic commercial core and tourist heart of Belém, home to the Ver-o-Peso market, the Estação das Docas riverfront, the Teatro da Paz and Belle Époque facades; busy and atmospheric by day but quiet and best avoided on foot after dark.

Belém's oldest quarter, where the city was founded, with the Forte do Presépio, the Mangal das Garças park, colonial churches and the Casa das Onze Janelas; rich in history and river views, sleepy at night.

One of Belém's most affluent and safest districts, built around the Basílica de Nazaré (heart of the Círio de Nazaré procession), with leafy mango-shaded streets, restaurants and the best hotels; a comfortable, central base for first-timers.
A modern, upscale-bohemian riverside neighborhood of high-rises, bars, restaurants and shopping malls; lively in the evenings and popular with visitors wanting nightlife and dining.
A quiet, leafy residential district next to Nazaré, centered on its namesake garden square; upscale and safe, close to downtown attractions but calmer, good for families.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water rather than from the tap.

transit.pay: City bus and BRT fares are paid in cash to the onboard conductor or with a rechargeable transit card (about R$3.60 a ride); river-boat fares are paid at the dock.
transit.hours: City buses run roughly 5am to midnight; the BRT corridor keeps similar hours, and river boats follow their own daytime-heavy schedules.
transit.note: Belém has no metro or tram. The backbone is the Grande Belém municipal bus network and a metropolitan BRT corridor, while boats and ferries along the Amazon delta connect the city to Ilha do Combu, Marajó Island and river communities.

landmarks: Ver-o-Peso Market
Latin America's largest open-air market sprawls along the waterfront under iron turrets, heaving with Amazonian fish, açaí, medicinal herbs and pungent tropical color.
Basílica Santuário de Nazaré
This opulent marble basilica houses the tiny miraculous image of Our Lady of Nazareth, focus of the Círio de Nazaré, one of the world's largest religious processions.
Estação das Docas
Three converted iron port warehouses now host riverside restaurants, breweries and galleries, where original cranes frame sunset views over Guajará Bay.
Theatro da Paz
A neoclassical jewel of the rubber boom era, this 1878 opera house dazzles with Italian frescoes, crystal chandeliers and gilded balconies overlooking Praça da República.
Forte do Presépio
The star-shaped riverside fort where Belém was founded in 1616 guards the bay with rows of cannon and a museum of the city's colonial origins.
Mangal das Garças
A lush riverside park alive with scarlet ibis and herons, its Belém lighthouse-style observation tower delivers sweeping views over the old town and river.
Catedral da Sé (Belém Cathedral)
Facing the fort across colonial Praça Frei Caetano Brandão, this eighteenth-century cathedral pairs a sober baroque facade with a lavish marble-rich interior.
Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi
Brazil's oldest Amazonian research institution doubles as a shady zoo-botanical garden where manatees, harpy eagles and giant water lilies preview the surrounding rainforest.
Cidade Velha (Old Town)
Belém's cradle of azulejo-fronted mansions and cobbled lanes rewards slow wandering between baroque churches, antique shops and crumbling Portuguese colonial grandeur.
Ilha do Combu
A short boat hop across the river, this jungle island tempts with riverside restaurants, artisanal chocolate makers and a taste of ribeirinho Amazon life.

train.note: No passenger railway serves Belém - Brazil has no intercity rail network and the Amazon region has none at all. Travel in and out is by riverboat, coach or plane.

bus.note: No international coaches. The Rodoviária de Belém has services south to São Luís (about 12 hours) and on toward Fortaleza and Brasília on Boa Esperança and Guanabara, bookable through ClickBus (https://www.clickbus.com.br/). There is no road west to Manaus, so that connection has to be made by boat or plane.

ferry.note: Belém's Terminal Hidroviário near the old town is the eastern gateway to the Amazon river network. The long hauls to Santarém and Manaus are hammock-deck boats taking several days; the Marajó Island crossing is a short and popular day trip. Everything is domestic - there is no international sailing from Belém. Buy tickets at the terminal a day or two ahead.

full.name: Ilha de Marajó
full.blurb: The world's largest river-and-ocean island at the mouth of the Amazon, reached by ferry, known for water buffalo ranches and quiet beaches.

full.name: Algodoal
full.blurb: A car-free fishing village on the Atlantic coast with dunes, tidal pools, and beaches reached by boat and a stretch of driving on sand.
